title: Ariadne's Thread
text:
King Minos of Crete had defeated Athens and demanded a cruel tribute: every few years the Athenians had to send seven young men and seven young women to Crete. There they were sent into the Labyrinth, the vast maze built by the craftsman Daedalus, where the Minotaur, a monster with the body of a man and the head of a bull, lived. None ever came out.

Theseus, son of the king of Athens, volunteered to go with the victims. In Crete, Minos's daughter Ariadne saw him and fell in love. She knew that even if Theseus could kill the Minotaur, he would never find his way out of the Labyrinth, whose passages were made to confuse anyone who entered. So she gave him a ball of thread.

Theseus tied one end of the thread at the entrance and unwound it as he went deeper and deeper into the maze. In its depths he found the Minotaur and killed it. Then, instead of wandering lost among the endless turns, he simply followed the thread back the way he had come and walked out into the daylight, leading the young Athenians with him.

He sailed away with Ariadne, though, in the best known version, he left her behind on the island of Naxos.
lesson: Before you go into a complicated situation, secure your way back out. A simple line to retrace is worth more than strength once you are lost.
date: Greek myth; Ovid 8 AD, Plutarch c. 100 AD
source: Plutarch, Life of Theseus; Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 8
caveat: Ancient authors give several versions of the myth; Plutarch himself records conflicting accounts.
